Context/Background:
Cancer-induced systemic inflammation is a dominant feature of cancer progression and metastatic spread. Clinically, systemic accumulation of myeloid cells is strongly correlated to poor prognosis in multiple solid malignancies, including breast cancer and a high neutrophil-to-lymphocyte (NLR) ratio is consistently associated with adverse outcomes. We, and others, previously published that primary tumors induce systemic accumulation and activation of neutrophils leading to enhanced metastatic spread in preclinical mouse models. In steady state, hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) give rise to all circulating blood cells through a series of progressively restrictive differentiation steps regulated by coordinated and temporal expression of transcription factors (TFs), leading to balanced bone marrow (BM) output. However, the molecular processes driving chronic, cancer-induced hematopoiesis, which leads to systemic inflammation, remain poorly understood.

We have previously demonstrated that expansion of metastasis-supporting neutrophils in mammary tumor-bearing K14cre;Cdh1fl/fl;Trp53fl/fl (KEP) mice is driven by an inflammatory cascade in which tumor associated macrophage (TAM)-derived IL-1β leads to elevated serum levels of G-CSF, the principal instructor of neutrophil generation. To understand how and at what stage of differentiation tumors drive neutrophil expansion, we clustered the genes upregulated in tumor-bearing mice based on their dynamics along the neutrophil pseudotime trajectory. We identified three groups of differentially expressed genes in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) from KEP mice, which we termed early, middle, and late, based on their expression patterns. 

Early genes showed significant enrichment of an HSC-specific gene set. Upregulated early genes were overexpressed in HSCs and multipotent progenitors (MPPs) from KEP mice compared to cells from control mice but were repressed in cells that were further along the inferred neutrophil differentiation trajectory. Middle genes were defined as genes that were expressed around the transition from MPP to granulocyte monocyte progenitor (GMP). Lastly, upregulated/downregulated late genes, expressed in late GMP, granulocyte progenitor (GP), and pro-neutrophil (ProNeu) populations, were found to be expressed prematurely and at a higher level in progenitors from KEP mice.
Prompt: Provide a summary of the relevant pathways and genes that are up and down regulated in KEP vs WT mice in early, intermediate and late neutrophil development, focusing on how and at what stage of differentiation tumors drive neutrophil expansion.
output_text:
Introduction/Context  
KEP mice (K14cre;Cdh1fl/fl;Trp53fl/fl) bearing mammary tumors exhibit systemic neutrophil expansion driven by TAM‐derived IL-1β and elevated G-CSF. Single‐cell pseudotime analysis of HSPCs from KEP versus WT mice defined three differentiation stages—early (HSC/MPP), intermediate (MPP→GMP), and late (late GMP/GP/ProNeu)—with 1,142 genes clustering into “Up” or “Down” groups per stage. Fold‐changes, p-values, and exact cell counts are not specified in the provided data.

Keywords  
• neutrophil differentiation  
• IL-1β/G-CSF axis  
• JAK-STAT signaling  
• telomere maintenance  
• mTORC1/Myc signaling  

Candidate Genes  
STAT3, JAK3, SOCS3, SOCS1, CEBPA, CEBPE

| p53 Pathway         | Down Late          | CEBPA;BTG1;CCND2;ZBTB16;TAP1                    |

Analysis  
Early progenitors switch on cytokine‐driven JAK-STAT and interferon‐γ modules (Up Early) while suppressing Rac signaling and endothelial niche signals (Down Early), consistent with a tumor-driven emergency granulopoiesis. During the MPP→GMP transition, KEP mice prematurely activate telomere maintenance and protein‐localization programs (Up Intermediate) and repress metabolic and MAPK pathways along with NK‐cell functions (Down Intermediate). In late GMP/ProNeu cells, tumors induce anabolic mTORC1/Myc and ER‐stress responses to fuel massive neutrophil output, while downregulating antigen‐presentation and BCR signaling (Down Late). This stage-specific reprogramming traces a path by which tumors co‐opt early cytokine circuits and late biosynthetic machinery to expand neutrophil production.

Targeted (keyword-guided) subset  
Filtering Up Early GO_BP terms for “Interleukin” isolated 9 interleukin-related signals such as Interleukin-2/15-mediated signaling (STAT3;JAK3;IL2RG), highlighting IL-1β/G-CSF cross-talk with JAK–STAT as an early driver.

Key Genes/Proteins (leading edge)  

Up  
| Gene   | Direction | Role/Function                                | Pathway(s)                                   |
|--------|-----------|----------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| STAT3  | Up Early  | TF mediating cytokine/JAK–STAT signaling     | IL-2/IL-15, interferon γ, IL-6/JAK/STAT3     |
| JAK3   | Up Early  | Kinase in common γ-chain cytokine receptors | IL-2/IL-15, JAK–STAT axis                    |
| SOCS3  | Up Early  | Negative feedback on cytokine signaling      | IL-6/JAK/STAT3, receptor signaling regulation|
| IL1R1  | Up Early  | IL-1 receptor initiating inflammation        | IL-6/JAK/STAT3                               |

Down  
| Gene   | Direction         | Role/Function                             | Pathway(s)                |
|--------|-------------------|-------------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| CEBPA  | Down Intermediate | Master TF for early myeloid commitment     | p53 signaling; apoptosis  |
| CEBPE  | Down Intermediate | Drives terminal granulocyte maturation     | p53 signaling; apoptosis  |
| CEBPB  | Up Late           | Links stress response to proliferation    | Integrated Stress Response; mTORC1 |

Comparisons  
Patterns differ from lymphoid organs where antigen‐presentation programs persist; here, neutrophil modules dominate. Single‐modality enrichments (e.g., telomere maintenance only in intermediate) may not generalize to other cell types.

Implications  
Early targeting of the IL-1β/G-CSF→JAK–STAT axis (e.g., anti–IL-1β, JAK inhibitors) could arrest progenitor activation. Late-stage blockade of mTORC1 or Myc may curtail excessive neutrophil output without compromising baseline hematopoiesis.

Next Steps & Clarification  
1. Validate cell‐cycle checkpoint engagement in early HSCs (e.g., mitotic nuclear membrane disassembly).  
2. Probe ER‐stress/unfolded protein responses in late GMP/ProNeu by single‐cell ATAC‐seq.  
3. Assess mitochondrial protein targeting and translation rates in ProNeu.  
4. Test telomerase inhibitors in intermediate progenitors for effects on neutrophil lineage skewing.
